slides.body:
Unit Outline

Part 1: Muscle Tissue
Part 2: The Muscular System (nomenclature)

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes: In this unit, we will first discuss the properties of the three main types of muscle tissue, and then we will discuss the naming of skeletal muscles of the body.

slides.title: Part 1: Muscle tissue
slides.body:
Part 1: Muscle tissue

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes: We begin with Part 1: Muscle tissue.

slides.title: Part 1: Muscle tissue
slides.body:
Part 1: Muscle tissue

3 muscle types:
skeletal
most move skeleton
controlled by nervous system
cardiac
pump blood through circulatory system
influenced by nervous system & hormones
smooth
involuntary movements
influenced by nervous system & hormones

Types of muscle. Adapted from: www.scientificanimations.com, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Muscle is one of the four primary tissue types of the body. When most people think of muscles, they think of the muscles that are visible just under the skin, particularly of the limbs. These are skeletal muscles, so-named because most of them move the skeleton. But there are two other types of muscle in the body, with distinctly different jobs. Cardiac muscle, found in the heart, is concerned with pumping blood through the circulatory system. Smooth muscle is concerned with various involuntary movements, such as having one’s hair stand on end when cold or frightened, or moving food through the digestive system. 

While the nervous system can influence the excitability of cardiac and smooth muscle to some degree, skeletal muscle completely depends on signaling from the nervous system to work properly. On the other hand, both cardiac muscle and smooth muscle can respond to other stimuli, such as hormones and local stimuli.

slides.title: Part 1: Muscle tissue
slides.body:
Part 1: Muscle tissue

Overview of muscle tissues
excitability - plasma membranes can change electrical states (polarized to depolarized) and send an electrical wave (action potential) along entire length of the membrane
contractility – can actively shorten
elasticity – can return to resting length (relax), due to elastic fibres
extensibility – can be passively stretched to extend

Muscle excitability. Adapted from: Ian Alexander, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
All three muscle tissues have some properties in common; they all exhibit a quality called excitability as their plasma membranes can change their electrical states (from polarized to depolarized) and send an electrical wave called an action potential along the entire length of the membrane. 

Contractility is the property that allows muscle tissue to actively pull on its attachment points and shorten. This process of muscle contraction (shortening) and relaxation (returning to its resting length) will be studied in the next unit. 

A muscle can return to its original length when relaxed due to a quality of muscle tissue called elasticity, whereby it can recoil to its original length due to the presence of elastic fibres. 

Muscle tissue also has the quality of extensibility. That is, it can be stretched, passively, when acted on by another force (remember that muscles only contract, they cannot extend themselves).

Skeletal muscle close-up. Credit: Berkshire Community College  Bioscience Image Library, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

The Three Types of Muscle Tissue. The body contains three types of muscle tissue: (a) skeletal muscle, (b) smooth muscle, and (c) cardiac muscle. From top, LM × 1600, LM × 1600, LM × 1600. (Micrographs provided by the Regents of University of Michigan Medical School © 2012)

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Striation

Differences among the three muscle types include the microscopic organization of their contractile proteins—actin and myosin. The actin and myosin proteins are arranged very regularly in the cytoplasm of individual muscle cells (referred to as fibres) in both skeletal muscle and cardiac muscle, which creates a pattern of stripes, called striations. The striations are visible with a light microscope under high magnification. 

Because the actin and myosin are not arranged in such regular fashion in smooth muscle, the cytoplasm of a smooth muscle fibre has a uniform, nonstriated appearance (resulting in the name smooth muscle). However, the less organized appearance of smooth muscle should not be interpreted as less efficient.

slides.notes:
Electrical coupling

Cardiac muscle fibres are physically and electrically connected to each other so that the entire heart contracts as one unit (called a syncytium). Some smooth muscle fibres are also electrically coupled to form smooth muscle sheets, while other smooth muscle cells are not coupled and are controlled individually.

slides.title: Part 1: Muscle tissue
slides.body:
Part 1: Muscle tissue

We will focus on skeletal muscles for the remainder of this unit…
Skeletal muscle functions
cause movement
maintain posture
stabilize joints and skeletal stability
allow for voluntary control of bodily functions at entry to and exit from body
protect organs
maintain temperature homeostasis
ATP hydrolysis and friction

Major muscles of the body. Anterior view. Right side: superficial. Left side: deep.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
The best-known feature of skeletal muscle is its ability to contract and cause movement. Skeletal muscles act not only to produce movement but also to stop movement, such as resisting gravity to maintain posture. Small, constant adjustments of the skeletal muscles are needed to hold a body upright or balanced in any position. Muscles also prevent excess movement of the bones and joints, maintaining skeletal stability and preventing skeletal structure damage or deformation. Joints can become misaligned or dislocated entirely by pulling on the associated bones; muscles work to keep joints stable. Skeletal muscles are located throughout the body at the openings of internal tracts to control the movement of various substances. These muscles allow functions, such as swallowing, urination, and defecation, to be under voluntary control. Skeletal muscles also protect internal organs (particularly abdominal and pelvic organs) by acting as an external barrier or shield to external trauma and by supporting the weight of the organs.

Skeletal muscles contribute to the maintenance of homeostasis in the body by generating heat. Muscle contraction requires energy, and when ATP is broken down, heat is produced. This heat is very noticeable during exercise, when sustained muscle movement causes body temperature to rise, and in cases of extreme cold, when shivering produces random skeletal muscle contractions to generate heat.

slides.title: Part 1: Muscle tissue
slides.body:
Part 1: Muscle tissue

Skeletal muscles are organs consisting of:
skeletal muscle fibers
blood vessels
nerve fibres
Deep fascia is a connective tissue sheath that separates skeletal muscles from one another and wraps together muscles, tendons, bones & cartilage
e.g., lumbar fascia binds deep muscles of back to spine and vertebrae, while servings as attachment point for more superficial muscles
vs. superficial fascia (a.k.a. hypodermis; covered in integumentary system unit), which holds skin onto muscle

Lumbar fascia. Credit: Sobotta and Playfair. Atlas and text-book of human anatomy. 1914. Internet Archive Book Images, No restrictions, via Wikimedia Commons

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Each skeletal muscle is an organ that consists of various integrated tissues. These tissues include the skeletal muscle fibres, blood vessels, nerve fibres, and connective tissue.

Skeletal muscles are separated from one another and wrapped together with their connected tendons, bones, and cartilage in connective tissue sheaths called the deep fascia. You have already heard of the superficial fascia, which is another term for the hypodermis, which we discussed in the integumentary system unit. The superficial fascia’s role is to attach the skin to the underlying muscle layers. The deep fascia discussed here, on the other hand, help to connect tissues of the musculoskeletal system at deeper levels of the body. An example is the lumbar fascia, shown here, which binds deep muscles of back to the spine and vertebrae, while servings as an attachment point for more superficial muscles.

Within these fascia, the skeletal muscles themselves are supported by three additional layers of connective tissue…

slides.title: Part 1: Muscle tissue
slides.body:
Part 1: Muscle tissue

Individual muscles have 3 layers of connective tissue collectively called mysia:
epimysium - sheath of dense, irregular connective tissue that wraps muscle and helps maintain its shape
perimysium – organizes muscle fibres into bundles called fascicles
allows for blood and nerves to reach muscle fibres through this connective tissue
nervous system can stimulate fascicles independently, to provided graded response
endomysium - collagen and reticular fibres encasing each muscle fibre
contains extracellular fluid that supports each muscle fibre

The Three Connective Tissue Layers. Bundles of muscle fibers, called fascicles, are covered by the perimysium. Muscle fibers are covered by the endomysium.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Skeletal muscles of the body are also individually wrapped in a layer of connective tissue, as are bundles of muscle fibres and individual muscle fibres within the muscle. These three layers of connective tissue, which enclose a muscle and provide structure to its components, are collectively called the “mysia”.

Each muscle is wrapped in a sheath of dense, irregular connective tissue called the epimysium, which allows a muscle to contract and move powerfully while maintaining its structural integrity. The epimysium also separates muscle from other tissues and organs in the area, allowing the muscle to move independently.

Inside each skeletal muscle, muscle fibres are organized into individual bundles, each called a fascicle, by a middle layer of connective tissue called the perimysium. This fascicular organization, common in muscles of the limbs, allows for blood and nerves to reach muscle fibres through this connective tissue. The fascicular organization also divides muscle fibres within a muscle into subgroups that can be independently activated by the nervous system, allowing for graded control of the strength of muscle contraction, based on what proportion of a muscle’s fascicles are activated.

Inside each fascicle, each muscle fibre is encased in a thin connective tissue layer of collagen and reticular fibres called the endomysium. The endomysium contains the extracellular fluid and nutrients to support the muscle fibre.

slides.title: Part 1: Muscle tissue
slides.body:
Part 1: Muscle tissue

Collagen in mysia of muscle connects to collagen of tendon, which connects to periosteum of bone
tension created by contraction of the muscle fibres is then transferred though the mysia, to the tendon, and then to the periosteum to pull on the bone for movement

Muscle, tendon, bone. Credit: Laboratoires Servier, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes: In skeletal muscles that work with tendons to pull on bones, the collagen in the three tissue layers of the mysia intertwines with the collagen of a tendon. At the other end of the tendon, it fuses with the periosteum coating the bone. The tension created by contraction of the muscle fibres is then transferred though the mysia, to the tendon, and then to the periosteum to pull on the bone for movement of the skeleton.

slides.title: Part 1: Muscle tissue
slides.body:
Part 1: Muscle tissue

Skeletal muscle fibres
large cells called fibres due to incredible length (up to 30 cm in sartorius)
due to fusion of (up to) hundreds of myoblasts

Sartorius Muscle. Credit: BodyParts3D/Anatomography, CC BY-SA 2.1 JP, via Wikimedia Commons

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Skeletal muscle fibres

Because skeletal muscle cells are long and cylindrical, they are commonly referred to as muscle fibres. Skeletal muscle fibres can be quite large for human cells, with diameters up to 100 μm and lengths up to 30 cm in the sartorius of the upper leg. During early development, embryonic myoblasts, each with its own nucleus, fuse with up to hundreds of other myoblasts to form each multinucleated skeletal muscle fibre. Multiple nuclei mean multiple copies of genes, permitting the production of the large amounts of proteins and enzymes needed for muscle contraction.

slides.title: Part 1: Muscle tissue
slides.body:
Part 1: Muscle tissue

Sarco (Greek: “flesh”) prefix:
sarcolemma
plasma membrane
sarcoplasm
cytoplasm
sarcoplasmic reticulum
endoplasmic reticulum
specialized for Ca2+ storage
sarcomere 
functional unit (contracts)

Muscle Fibre. A skeletal muscle fibre is surrounded by a plasma membrane called the sarcolemma, which contains sarcoplasm, the cytoplasm of muscle cells. A muscle fibre is composed of many fibrils, which give the cell its striated appearance.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Much of the terminology associated with muscle fibres is rooted in the Greek term sarco, which means “flesh.” 

The plasma membrane of muscle fibres is called the sarcolemma, the cytoplasm is referred to as sarcoplasm, and the specialized smooth endoplasmic reticulum, which stores, releases, and retrieves calcium ions is called the sarcoplasmic reticulum. 

The functional unit of a skeletal muscle fibre (the part causing its contraction) is the sarcomere, a highly organized arrangement of the contractile myofilaments.

slides.title: Part 1: Muscle tissue
slides.body:
Part 1: Muscle tissue

Sarcomere
functional unit of the muscle fibre
actin – thin myofilaments
myosin – thick myofilaments
regulatory proteins
troponin
tropomyosin
other support proteins
actin myofilaments are anchored by Z-discs (called Z-lines, because that is how they look in two-dimensional pictures)

The Sarcomere. The sarcomere, the region from one Z-line to the next Z-line, is the functional unit of a skeletal muscle fibre.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
As stated earlier, the striated appearance of skeletal muscle fibres is due to the arrangement of the actin and myosin myofilaments in sequential order, from one end of the muscle fibre to the other. Each packet of these microfilaments and their regulatory proteins, troponin and tropomyosin (along with other proteins) is called a sarcomere.

Because the actin and its troponin-tropomyosin complex (the function of which will be explained later) form strands that are thinner than the myosin, the actin is called the thin filament of the sarcomere. Likewise, because the myosin strands and their multiple heads have more mass and are thicker, they are called the thick filament of the sarcomere.

Each sarcomere is around 2 μm in length with a cylinder-like arrangement and is bordered by structures called Z-discs, to which the actin myofilaments are anchored. Z-disks are also called Z-lines, because that is how they look in two-dimensional pictures.

slides.title: Part 1: Muscle tissue
slides.body:
Part 1: Muscle tissue

Myofibril
long contractile segments of sarcomeres within muscle fibres
thousands can be found in a single muscle fibre

Muscle Fibre. A skeletal muscle fibre is surrounded by a plasma membrane called the sarcolemma, which contains sarcoplasm, the cytoplasm of muscle cells. A muscle fibre is composed of many fibrils, which give the cell its striated appearance.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes: The sarcomere is the functional unit of the muscle fibre. Each sarcomere is bundled within a myofibril that runs the entire length of the muscle fibre. As myofibrils contract, the entire muscle cell contracts. Because myofibrils are only about 1 μm in diameter, hundreds to thousands can be found inside one muscle fibre, like many strands lined up, side-by-side inside one bundle.

slides.notes:
Okay, now on to Part 2: The muscular system. 

Part 2 contains extensive coverage of skeletal muscle naming, location, and function. You will not be responsible for learning every skeletal muscle in the body—such an endeavour would be more appropriate for a laboratory course. Rather, here we will focus on the logic behind skeletal muscle names, and then cover some example muscles, which you will be expected to know.

slides.body:
Part 2: The muscular system

Naming Skeletal Muscles
Greeks and Romans conducted first studies on human body in Western culture
since then, anatomical naming uses Latin and Greek terminology
Etymology 
study of how the root of a word entered a language and how the use of the word evolved over time
can help with memorization of muscle names

“The Anatomy Lesson of Dr. Nicolaes Tulp” by Rembrandt. Credit: Rembrandt, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Naming Skeletal Muscles

The Greeks and Romans conducted the first studies done on the human body in Western culture, leading to the application of Latin and Greek terminology or roots in the naming of the skeletal muscles. The large number of muscles in the body and unfamiliar words can make learning the names of the muscles in the body seem daunting, but understanding the etymology can help. Etymology is the study of how the root of a particular word entered a language and how the use of the word evolved over time.

slides.title: Part 2: The muscular system
slides.body:
Part 2: The muscular system

Understanding muscle names will help you remember location and function
e.g., abductor digiti minimi moves the little finger or toe away from the others (the movement of abduction)
e.g., adductor digiti minimi moves the little finger or toe toward the other digits (the movement of adduction)

Understanding a Muscle Name from its Latin Roots

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Taking the time to learn the root of the words is crucial to understanding the vocabulary of anatomy and physiology. When you understand the names of muscles it will help you remember where the muscles are located and what they do.

For example, this table contrasts the abductor digiti minimi and the adductor digiti minimi. Note that ab means away from, while ad means toward. A duct moves something. Digiti refers to your digits (fingers and toes). Minimi means tiny, or minimal. Hence, from these names, you can deduce that an abductor digiti minimi moves the little finger or toe away from the others (the movement of abduction), while the adductor digiti minimi works in opposition and moves the little finger or toe toward the other digits (the movement of adduction).
